visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Laws and policies are only words until someone carries them out. In this part we study the executive, the organ that does this. We compare three types of executive, look at how the President of India is elected, what the office can and cannot do, and the role of the Vice-President.

slides.heading: What is the executive?

rows: The organ of government that implements laws and policies
The elected and temporary part: ministers and the head of government
Civil servants, who stay in service when governments change

visual.alt: Table of terms: the executive implements laws and policies; the political executive is the elected and temporary ministers and head of government; the permanent executive is the civil servants

slides.narration: The executive is the organ of government that implements laws and policies. It has two parts. The political executive is the elected and temporary part: the ministers and the head of government. The permanent executive is made up of civil servants, who stay in service whichever party governs.

Parliamentary, for example the United Kingdom and India: a nominal head of state, a Prime Minister who is answerable to the legislature. Semi-presidential, for example France: an elected President and a Prime Minister who is answerable to the legislature
visual.caption: Three types of executive compared.

slides.narration: Countries organise the executive in different ways. In a presidential system, as in the United States, the President is head of state and head of government. In a parliamentary system, as in the United Kingdom and India, the head of government answers to the legislature, and the head of state is nominal. In a semi presidential system, as in France, there is both an elected President and a Prime Minister.

slides.body_md: Use the features of three imagined countries to name the type of executive.
bullets: To whom is that person answerable?

rows: Directly elected President leads state and government; fixed term
Chancellor needs the Assembly majority; ceremonial head of state
Directly elected President and a Prime Minister answerable to the Council

visual.alt: Worked example table classifying three imagined countries: Arvelia is presidential, Brendoria is parliamentary and Calvaris is semi-presidential
visual.caption: Ask: who is head of government, and to whom is that person answerable?

slides.narration: Let us classify three imagined countries. In Arvelia, a directly elected President leads both state and government for a fixed term, so it is presidential. In Brendoria, the Chancellor needs the Assembly majority and the head of state is ceremonial, so it is parliamentary. Calvaris has an elected President and a Prime Minister answerable to the Council, so it is semi presidential.

slides.heading: India: a nominal head and a real executive

nodes.label: Executive power is vested in the President
It is exercised in the President's name
In practice the Council of Ministers exercises it
The President is the nominal head

visual.alt: Flow: executive power is vested in the President and exercised in the President's name, but in practice the Council of Ministers exercises it, so the President is the nominal head
visual.caption: Nominal and real executive

slides.narration: India has a parliamentary executive. The Constitution vests executive power in the President, and it is exercised in the President's name. But in practice it is exercised by the Council of Ministers. That is why the President is called the nominal or constitutional head, while the Prime Minister and the Council form the real executive.

visual.caption: How the President is elected.

slides.narration: The President is not elected directly by the voters. The elected members of the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies form an electoral college. The Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry are included. Members vote by secret ballot, using proportional representation by single transferable vote. Nominated members do not vote in this election.

slides.heading: The electoral college, term and removal

rows: Elected members of both Houses and of the State Legislative Assemblies, with Delhi and Puducherry
Nominated members; members of Legislative Councils; ordinary voters
Proportional representation by single transferable vote; secret ballot
Five years; impeachment for violation of the Constitution

visual.alt: Table about the election of the President: indirect election by an electoral college of elected members of both Houses and of State Legislative Assemblies, with Delhi and Puducherry; nominated members and ordinary voters do not vote; proportional representation by single transferable vote; five-year term; impeachment for violating the Constitution

slides.narration: Here are the main points. The election is indirect, held by an electoral college of elected members. The method is proportional representation by single transferable vote. The term is five years. The President can be removed before that only by impeachment, for violating the Constitution. Ordinary voters, nominated members and members of State Legislative Councils do not vote.

slides.heading: Powers of the President

rows: Appoints the Prime Minister, judges, Governors and other officials
Gives assent to bills; issues ordinances; addresses Parliament
A money bill is introduced only on the President's recommendation
Can proclaim an emergency, on the advice of the Council of Ministers

visual.alt: Table of the powers of the President: executive, such as appointing the Prime Minister, judges and Governors; legislative, such as assent to bills and ordinances; financial, such as recommending money bills; emergency powers
visual.caption: All exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

slides.narration: The President has four kinds of powers. Executive powers include appointing the Prime Minister, judges and Governors. Legislative powers include giving assent to bills, issuing ordinances and addressing Parliament. Financial powers include recommending money bills. Emergency powers let the President proclaim an emergency. All are exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

slides.heading: Acting on the advice of ministers

nodes.label: 1950: the Constitution begins; the President acts on advice in practice
1976, 42nd Amendment: the advice is binding
1978, 44th Amendment: the President may return the advice once
If it is sent back, the President must act on it

visual.alt: Flow: from 1950 the President acts on advice in practice, the 42nd Amendment in 1976 makes the advice binding, the 44th Amendment in 1978 lets the President return it once, and if it is sent back the President must act on it
visual.caption: Advice of the ministers

slides.narration: In practice the President has long acted on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The forty second Amendment of nineteen seventy six made that advice binding. The forty fourth Amendment of nineteen seventy eight lets the President return the advice once for reconsideration. If the Council sends the same advice back, the President must act on it.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a hung House
slides.body_md: No party or alliance has a clear majority after an imagined general election. Trace what happens.
bullets: The President **judges** who can command a majority

rows: Three alliances win fewer than half the seats in the Lok Sabha
The President meets the leaders and asks for letters of support
The President invites the leader most likely to command a majority
The new government must prove its majority in the Lok Sabha

visual.alt: Worked example table of a hung House: three alliances win fewer than half the seats; the President meets the leaders and asks for letters of support; the President invites the leader most likely to command a majority; the government proves its majority in the Lok Sabha
visual.caption: Discretion is real, but limited by the House.

slides.narration: Imagine three alliances, each with fewer than half of the seats. The President meets their leaders and asks for letters of support. Then the President invites the leader who seems most likely to command a majority. The new government must prove its majority in the Lok Sabha. The President's discretion is real, but the House has the final word.

slides.heading: Discretion in practice

rows: Return it once for reconsideration; then act on it
Delay assent, since no time limit is set (the pocket veto)
Judge who is most likely to command majority support

visual.alt: Table of the three situations of the President's discretion in practice: returning the advice once, delaying assent to an ordinary bill (the pocket veto), and choosing a Prime Minister when no party has a clear majority

slides.narration: The President has limited discretion in three situations. First, the advice of the ministers can be returned once for reconsideration. Second, assent to an ordinary bill can be delayed, because the Constitution fixes no time limit. Third, when no party or alliance has a clear majority, the President uses judgment in choosing the Prime Minister.

slides.heading: The pocket veto

nodes.label: Parliament passes an ordinary bill
The bill reaches the President
The President neither signs nor returns it; no time limit applies
The bill stays pending: a pocket veto

visual.alt: Flow of the pocket veto: Parliament passes an ordinary bill, it reaches the President, the President neither signs nor returns it as no time limit applies, and the bill stays pending
visual.caption: The pocket veto

slides.narration: The pocket veto is one use of this discretion. Parliament passes an ordinary bill, and it reaches the President. The Constitution sets no time limit for assent. So the President may neither sign nor return the bill, and it stays pending. This practice is called the pocket veto. Different views are held on how far it should be used.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the practice
slides.body_md: A passed bill is neither signed nor returned and stays with the President for years. What is this called?
slides.narration: Think of a veto that works by taking no action.

slides.heading: The Vice-President

rows: By the members of both Houses of Parliament
Ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Acts as President when the office is vacant

visual.alt: Table about the Vice-President: elected by the members of both Houses, five-year term, ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and acts as President when the office is vacant

slides.narration: The Vice-President is elected by the members of both Houses of Parliament, for a term of five years. The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, which means the office carries this role automatically. The Vice-President also acts as President when that office is vacant, until the vacancy is filled.

slides.heading: Quick check: who acts?
slides.body_md: The President resigns. Who acts as President until the vacancy is filled?
slides.narration: Recall the second role of the Vice-President.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Nominal head; electoral college; single transferable vote; five years; impeachment
Return advice; pocket veto; choice of Prime Minister in a hung House
Elected by both Houses; Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; acts as President

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: three types of executive, the President as nominal head, the amendments on advice, areas of discretion and the Vice-President

slides.narration: To sum up. The executive implements laws and policies. Executives are presidential, parliamentary or semi presidential. In India the President is the nominal head, elected by an electoral college by single transferable vote for five years. The forty second and forty fourth Amendments shape the advice of ministers. The President has limited discretion, and the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha.

visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: The real work of the executive is done by the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers, and by the civil servants who carry out their decisions. In this part we study how the ministers are appointed and held to account, and how the permanent executive is organised and recruited.

slides.heading: The Prime Minister

rows: Leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha
Appointed on the Prime Minister's advice

visual.alt: Table about the Prime Minister: appointed by the President, leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha, ministers appointed on the Prime Minister's advice, responsible to the Lok Sabha

slides.narration: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President and is usually the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha. The other ministers are appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are responsible to the Lok Sabha, which can remove them if it loses confidence in them.

slides.heading: The Council of Ministers

rows: Senior ministers; the inner group that takes major decisions
Junior ministers, helping or in charge of some departments

visual.alt: Table of the three ranks in the Council of Ministers: Cabinet Ministers, the inner group; Ministers of State; and Deputy Ministers who assist
visual.caption: A minister who is not an MP must become one within six months.

slides.narration: The Council of Ministers has three ranks. Cabinet Ministers are the senior ministers and form the inner group. Ministers of State are junior ministers, and Deputy Ministers assist. A person who is not a member of Parliament can become a minister, but must become a member of either House within six months.

sections.heading: 1. The executive and its types
sections.body_md:
The **executive** is the organ of government that **implements laws and policies**. The **political executive** is elected and temporary: the ministers and the head of government. The **permanent executive** is the civil servants.

Three types are commonly distinguished.
- **Presidential**, for example the United States: the President is head of state and of government and is elected by the people for a fixed term.
- **Parliamentary**, for example the United Kingdom and India: the Prime Minister and Cabinet are responsible to the legislature, and the head of state is nominal.
- **Semi-presidential**, for example France: there is both a directly elected President and a Prime Minister.

The elected and temporary part of the executive: the ministers and the head of government.
The civil servants, who remain in service when governments change.
A system in which the head of government and the Cabinet are responsible to the legislature and the head of state is nominal.

sections.heading: 2. The President of India
sections.body_md:
The President is the **nominal (constitutional) head**: executive power is exercised in the President's name, but in practice by the Council of Ministers.

- **Election:** indirect, by an **electoral college** of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies, including those of Delhi and Puducherry. Voting is by **proportional representation by single transferable vote**.
- **Term and removal:** five years; **impeachment** for violation of the Constitution.
- **Powers:** executive (appointing the Prime Minister, judges, Governors), legislative (assent to bills, ordinances, addressing Parliament), financial and emergency powers.

sections.heading: 3. Advice of ministers and discretion
sections.body_md:
The President must act on the **advice of the Council of Ministers**. The **42nd Amendment (1976)** made the advice binding; the **44th Amendment (1978)** allows the President to **return the advice once** for reconsideration, after which the President must act on it.

Discretion in practice is limited: the President may **return the advice once**, **delay assent to an ordinary bill** (the **pocket veto**, since no time limit is set), and use judgment in **choosing a Prime Minister** when no party or alliance has a clear majority.

sections.heading: 4. Vice-President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
sections.body_md:
The **Vice-President** is elected by the members of both Houses, serves five years, is **ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** and **acts as President** when the office is vacant.

The **Prime Minister** is appointed by the President and is the **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha**. Ministers must be members of Parliament, or become members **within six months**. The Council is **collectively responsible** to the Lok Sabha; a **no-confidence motion** can remove the government. The **91st Amendment (2003)** limits the Council to **15 per cent** of the strength of the Lok Sabha. The **Cabinet** is the inner group of senior ministers. The influence of a Prime Minister is shaped by party position and by coalition conditions. Governors and Chief Ministers form a similar system in the states.

sections.heading: 5. The permanent executive
sections.body_md:
**Civil servants** are the permanent executive: recruited on **merit**, trained and **politically neutral**. They **implement policies** and **advise ministers**.

The services are the **All India Services** (for example the Indian Administrative Service and the Indian Police Service), recruited by the Union but serving in the states; the **Central Services**; and the **State Services**.

The **Union Public Service Commission** recruits for the Union services and **State Public Service Commissions** for the state services. Their members have **security of tenure**.

Services such as the IAS and IPS, recruited by the Union but serving in the states.

sections.heading: 6. Reservation and issues
sections.body_md:
The Constitution allows **reservation in recruitment** for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes. In direct recruitment to Union posts the shares are **15, 7.5 and 27 per cent** (as of 2024); states fix their own.

Issues that some people raise, with other views: **political interference** (some argue that pressure affects postings); **accountability to citizens** (some argue that officers are not directly accountable; others reply that they answer to ministers and the legislature); **red tape** (some argue that it delays work; others, that procedures protect fairness); the **need for responsiveness** (some argue for more, others that it must not cost neutrality).

Rigid adherence to procedures that causes delay.

- Letting nominated members vote for the President: they do not.

- Saying civil servants change with governments: they are permanent.

cards.back_md: Scheduled Castes 15, Scheduled Tribes 7.5, Other Backward Classes 27 per cent.

cards.front_md: Four issues some raise about the bureaucracy
cards.back_md: Political interference; accountability to citizens; red tape; the need for responsiveness.

questions.stem_md: Among the organs of government, the one mainly responsible for carrying out laws and putting policies into effect is the

options.text_md: legislature
executive
judiciary
electorate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** executive. The executive implements laws and policies. The legislature makes laws, the judiciary interprets them and settles disputes, and the electorate is the body of voters, not an organ of government.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined country of Dorsana, the Minister of Education is an elected member of the legislature, while the Director of Education is an officer who has served under four governments. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Both belong to the political executive
The Minister belongs to the permanent executive and the Director to the political executive
Both belong to the permanent executive
The Minister belongs to the political executive and the Director to the permanent executive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Minister belongs to the political executive and the Director to the permanent executive. An elected minister who holds office for a time is part of the political executive, while an officer who stays in service under successive governments is part of the permanent executive. The other options mix up or merge the two parts.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined country of Arvelia, voters directly elect a President for a fixed four-year term. The President is both head of state and head of government, names the ministers and cannot be removed by an ordinary vote of the legislature. Arvelia has a

options.text_md: presidential executive
parliamentary executive
semi-presidential executive
nominal executive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** presidential executive. One directly elected person who is both head of state and head of government, with a fixed term and no dependence on the legislature, is the mark of a presidential system. A parliamentary system makes the government answerable to the legislature, a semi-presidential one has a separate Prime Minister, and a nominal executive describes a ceremonial head.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined country of Brendoria, the Chancellor leads the government only as long as a majority of the Assembly supports the Cabinet, while a ceremonial Governor-General performs the duties of head of state. This is a

options.text_md: presidential executive
semi-presidential executive
parliamentary executive
permanent executive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** parliamentary executive. A government that depends on majority support in the legislature, with a ceremonial head of state, is parliamentary. There is no directly elected President, so it is neither presidential nor semi-presidential, and the permanent executive means civil servants.

questions.stem_md: The imagined republic of Calvaris has a President elected directly by the people. The President appoints a Prime Minister, and the Prime Minister and Cabinet must keep the confidence of the National Council. Calvaris has a

options.text_md: purely presidential executive
purely parliamentary executive with a nominal head
semi-presidential executive
permanent executive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** semi-presidential executive. A directly elected President together with a Prime Minister who answers to the legislature is the semi-presidential pattern, as in France. In a purely presidential system there is no such Prime Minister, and in a purely parliamentary one the head of state is not directly elected.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined town-hall discussion, Ravi says that every decision of the Union government is taken in the President's name, so the President personally decides everything. Which reply is closest to the Constitution?

options.text_md: Decisions are in the President's name, but in practice the Council of Ministers takes them, and the President is the nominal head
He is right, since the President can overrule the ministers at will
He is right, since the President chooses the ministers without any advice
He is wrong, because the President has no role in government at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Decisions are in the President's name, but in practice the Council of Ministers takes them, and the President is the nominal head. Executive power is exercised in the President's name but in practice by the Council of Ministers, so the President is the nominal head. The President does not overrule ministers at will, the ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister's advice, and the President does have a constitutional role.

questions.stem_md: The electoral college that elects the President of India consists of

options.text_md: all members of Parliament and all members of the State Legislative Councils
all voters registered on the electoral rolls of the country
the members of the Lok Sabha alone
the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies, including those of Delhi and Puducherry

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies, including those of Delhi and Puducherry. The college has the elected members of the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies, with the Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry included. Members of State Legislative Councils and nominated members are outside it, ordinary voters do not vote directly, and the Lok Sabha alone is too narrow.

questions.stem_md: Sunil Verma, a scientist in an imagined list, is nominated by the President to the Rajya Sabha for his work in science. In the next election of the President, he

options.text_md: can vote, like every other member of the Rajya Sabha
cannot vote, because only elected members are in the electoral college
can vote only if he joins a political party first
can vote, but his vote counts as half a vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** cannot vote, because only elected members are in the electoral college. Only elected members of the Houses and the State Legislative Assemblies vote for the President, so a nominated member has no vote in that election (he does vote in the Vice-President's election). Party membership and half-votes have no role.

questions.stem_md: The President of India can be removed before the five-year term ends through

options.text_md: impeachment for violation of the Constitution
a motion of no confidence in the Lok Sabha
dismissal by the Prime Minister on the advice of the Cabinet
a decision of the Election Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** impeachment for violation of the Constitution. The only way is impeachment, a process in Parliament for violating the Constitution. A no-confidence motion applies to the Council of Ministers, not the President, and neither the Prime Minister nor the Election Commission can remove the President.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined case, the President returns the advice of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration. The Council reconsiders and sends back the same advice. What must the President now do?

options.text_md: return it a second time
act in accordance with the advice
dismiss the Council of Ministers
refer the advice to the Supreme Court for a binding decision

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** act in accordance with the advice. The 44th Amendment (1978) lets the President return the advice once; if it is sent back, the President must act on it. A second return, dismissal and a binding reference to the Supreme Court are not provided for.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly pairs the amendment with its effect on the President's relation with the ministers?

options.text_md: The 44th Amendment (1978) made the advice binding; the 42nd Amendment (1976) let the President return it once
The 42nd Amendment (1976) removed the need for advice; the 44th Amendment (1978) restored it
The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the ministers' advice binding; the 44th Amendment (1978) let the President return it once for reconsideration
The 91st Amendment (2003) made the advice binding; the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the Cabinet

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the ministers' advice binding; the 44th Amendment (1978) let the President return it once for reconsideration. The 42nd Amendment made the advice binding and the 44th softened this by allowing one return for reconsideration. The other options reverse the order, claim advice was ever removed, or credit the 91st Amendment, which limited the size of the Council of Ministers.

questions.stem_md: A bill passed by both Houses in an imagined session reaches the President, who neither gives assent nor returns it, and the bill stays with the President for years. Because the Constitution sets no time limit, this practice is called

options.text_md: an ordinance
impeachment
a vote of confidence
a pocket veto

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a pocket veto. Keeping an ordinary bill without a decision, when no time limit applies, is the pocket veto. An ordinance is a law the President issues when Parliament is not in session, impeachment is removal of the President, and a confidence vote concerns the government in the Lok Sabha.

questions.stem_md: After an imagined general election, no party and no alliance wins more than half the seats in the Lok Sabha. In choosing a Prime Minister, the President is then most free to use

options.text_md: the right to appoint anyone, whether or not that person has support in the House
the power to set aside all the parties and rule directly
the advice of the outgoing Council of Ministers alone
personal judgment about who is most likely to command majority support

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** personal judgment about who is most likely to command majority support. When no party or alliance has a clear majority, the President must judge who can command the confidence of the House, which is where discretion is real. The President cannot ignore the House, cannot rule directly, and need not rely only on the outgoing council.

questions.stem_md: The Vice-President of India is, by virtue of office, the

options.text_md: Speaker of the Lok Sabha
head of the Council of Ministers
Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
leader of the opposition

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, the Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers, and the leader of the opposition is a separate post.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined event, the President of India resigns and the office falls vacant. Who acts as President until the vacancy is filled?

options.text_md: The Prime Minister
The Vice-President
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Cabinet Secretary

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Vice-President. The Vice-President acts as President when the office is vacant. The Prime Minister, the Speaker and the Cabinet Secretary have no such role in this situation.

questions.stem_md: The Prime Minister of India is

options.text_md: appointed by the President, usually as the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha
elected directly by all voters in a national vote
elected by the same electoral college that elects the President
chosen by the Rajya Sabha from among its own members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** appointed by the President, usually as the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha. The President appoints the Prime Minister, who is normally the leader of the majority party or alliance in the Lok Sabha. The Prime Minister is not elected directly or by the electoral college, and the Rajya Sabha does not choose the Prime Minister.

questions.stem_md: Ananya Rao, who is not a member of either House of Parliament, is invited to join the Union Council of Ministers in an imagined government. To continue as a minister she must

options.text_md: win a Lok Sabha seat within one year
become a member of either House within six months
resign after three months and be reappointed
be nominated to the Rajya Sabha by the Vice-President

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** become a member of either House within six months. A person who is not a member of Parliament can be a minister, but must become a member of either House within six months. The one-year and three-month limits are invented, and the Vice-President does not nominate members.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined government, the Minister of Roads takes a decision that the Lok Sabha strongly opposes, and the House passes its motion against the whole Council of Ministers and not against the Minister of Roads alone. This follows from the principle of

options.text_md: judicial review
federalism
the pocket veto
collective responsibility

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** collective responsibility. Under collective responsibility the whole Council answers to the Lok Sabha for the decisions of any minister, so the House can act against all of them together. Judicial review, federalism and the pocket veto are unrelated to the relationship between the House and the ministers.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined session, the Lok Sabha passes a motion of no confidence against the government. Under the system of collective responsibility,

options.text_md: the Council of Ministers must resign
the Prime Minister alone resigns while the other ministers stay
the Rajya Sabha decides whether the government may continue
the President is removed from office

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the Council of Ministers must resign. Because the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, loss of its confidence means the whole Council must resign. It is not only the Prime Minister, the Rajya Sabha has no such say, and the President is not affected.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Dharmpal has a Legislative Assembly of 200 members. Under the 91st Amendment (2003), which limits the Council of Ministers to 15 per cent of the strength of the House, the Council of Ministers including the Chief Minister can have at most

options.text_md: 15 members
20 members
30 members
50 members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 30 members. Fifteen per cent of 200 is 30. The numbers 15 and 20 do not follow from the rule, and 50 would be a quarter of the House, which is more than the limit allows.

questions.stem_md: In the Union Council of Ministers, the inner group of senior ministers that takes the major policy decisions is the

options.text_md: group of Ministers of State
group of Deputy Ministers
Cabinet
electoral college

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Cabinet. The Cabinet is the inner group of senior ministers. Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers are junior ranks of the Council, and the electoral college is the body that elects the President.

questions.stem_md: The system in the states is similar to that at the Union. The nominal head of a state and the real executive head are, respectively,

options.text_md: the Governor and the Chief Minister with the Council of Ministers
the Chief Minister and the Governor
the Speaker and the Chief Minister
the Chief Justice and the Governor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the Governor and the Chief Minister with the Council of Ministers. The Governor is the nominal head, like the President, and the Chief Minister with the Council of Ministers is the real executive. The other pairings reverse the roles or bring in the Speaker and a judge, who are not heads of the executive.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined governments of the same country have Prime Ministers whose influence differs: one leads a party with a clear majority, the other leads a coalition of several parties. Which explanation best fits the difference?

options.text_md: The Constitution gives a coalition Prime Minister a different set of powers
A Prime Minister whose party has a majority is not responsible to the Lok Sabha
The President decides how much influence each Prime Minister has
The Prime Minister's actual influence depends partly on party position and on how many partners must be satisfied

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Prime Minister's actual influence depends partly on party position and on how many partners must be satisfied. The Constitution gives the same position to every Prime Minister; what varies is the political setting, such as the size of the majority, the hold over the party and the need to keep coalition partners together. No Prime Minister is outside responsibility to the Lok Sabha, and the President does not allot influence.

questions.stem_md: The permanent executive in India consists of

options.text_md: the Prime Minister and the Cabinet
civil servants
the members of the Lok Sabha
the President and the Vice-President

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** civil servants. Civil servants make up the permanent executive, since they stay in service when governments change. The Prime Minister, Cabinet and members of the Lok Sabha belong to the political side, and the President and Vice-President are constitutional offices.

questions.stem_md: A new party forms the government in the imagined state of Marenda. Secretary Anil Rao, who served the previous government, is asked to carry out the new government's very different housing policy, and he does so faithfully. His conduct is mainly an example of

options.text_md: the political neutrality expected of a civil servant
the collective responsibility of ministers
the discretion of the Governor
the impeachment of a minister

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the political neutrality expected of a civil servant. A civil servant serves whichever government is in office and carries out its policies impartially, which is political neutrality. Collective responsibility concerns ministers, and the discretion of the Governor and impeachment are unrelated to an officer's conduct.

questions.stem_md: The Indian Administrative Service and the Indian Police Service are examples of

options.text_md: Central Services
All India Services
State Services
municipal services

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** All India Services. These are All India Services: recruited by the Union but serving in the states. Central Services serve the Union government, State Services are recruited by the state, and municipal services belong to local bodies.

questions.stem_md: Recruitment to the Union services is conducted by the

options.text_md: Election Commission
Finance Commission
Union Public Service Commission
State Public Service Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Union Public Service Commission. The Union Public Service Commission recruits for the Union services. The Election Commission conducts elections, the Finance Commission advises on sharing revenues, and a State Public Service Commission recruits for the state services.

questions.stem_md: Sulochana wants to join the civil services of the imagined state of Ranmal, and not those of the Union. Which body conducts recruitment to the posts of that state?

options.text_md: The Union Public Service Commission
The Election Commission
The Council of Ministers of Ranmal
The Ranmal State Public Service Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Ranmal State Public Service Commission. Each state has a State Public Service Commission that recruits for its state services. The Union Public Service Commission serves the Union and All India Services, the Election Commission holds elections, and ministers decide policy and do not conduct recruitment.

questions.stem_md: Members of the Union and State Public Service Commissions are given security of tenure so that they can

options.text_md: remain in office for life whatever their conduct
be free of all rules of service
be chosen by the Prime Minister alone
recruit without fear of being removed by the government of the day

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** recruit without fear of being removed by the government of the day. Security of tenure means a member cannot be removed at will, which protects the Commission's independence in selecting candidates on merit. It does not mean immunity for misconduct, freedom from all rules, or selection by the Prime Minister alone.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Department of Water Supply of a state, the minister announces a plan to lay pipelines to 300 villages. Who is mainly responsible for working out the details and putting it into effect day to day?

options.text_md: The Chief Justice of the High Court
The Election Commission
The civil servants of the department, under the minister's direction
The voters of the 300 villages

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The civil servants of the department, under the minister's direction. The minister sets the policy and the civil servants of the department prepare and carry it out. The High Court, the Election Commission and the voters have no such administrative role.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, in direct recruitment to posts under the Union government, the reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes are respectively

options.text_md: 10 per cent, 5 per cent and 20 per cent
15 per cent, 7.5 per cent and 27 per cent
22.5 per cent, 15 per cent and 27 per cent
7.5 per cent, 15 per cent and 27 per cent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 15 per cent, 7.5 per cent and 27 per cent. The figures are 15, 7.5 and 27 per cent in that order. The second set is invented, the third inflates the first two, and the fourth swaps Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

questions.stem_md: Tarun passed the Union examination, joined the Indian Administrative Service and was posted to the imagined state of Kondar. He belongs to

options.text_md: the All India Services, recruited by the Union and serving in a state
the State Services, recruited by Kondar
the Central Services, serving only in Union ministries
the political executive, removable by the voters

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the All India Services, recruited by the Union and serving in a state. An officer of the Indian Administrative Service is a member of the All India Services: recruited by the Union, posted in states. He was not recruited by the state, does not serve only in the Union ministries, and as a civil servant is part of the permanent executive, not the political one.

questions.stem_md: Some argue that a district office in the imagined district of Tillanagar takes weeks to issue a simple certificate because every file passes through many desks and forms. Which concern about the bureaucracy does this illustrate?

options.text_md: political interference in postings
red tape, the rigid following of procedures that delays work
lack of merit in recruitment
lack of security of tenure for commission members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** red tape, the rigid following of procedures that delays work. Delay caused by many procedures and steps is called red tape. Political interference concerns pressure on officers from politicians, and merit in recruitment and tenure of commission members are not involved in the case.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The President of India is called a nominal head of the executive.

**Reason (R):** The President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers, which exercises executive power in practice.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because the real power rests with the Council of Ministers, the President is the nominal head.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A member whom the President nominates to the Rajya Sabha has no vote in the election of the President.

**Reason (R):** Only the elected members of the Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies form the electoral college.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: a nominated member is not an elected member, so he or she is outside the electoral college.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The President may in practice delay assent to an ordinary bill for an indefinite period.

**Reason (R):** The President is elected by an electoral college that includes members of the State Legislative Assemblies.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the delay is possible because the Constitution sets no time limit for assent, not because of how the President is elected.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Vice-President of India chairs the sittings of the Rajya Sabha.

**Reason (R):** The Vice-President is elected by the members of both Houses of Parliament.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha because the Constitution makes the office its ex officio Chairman, not because of who elects the Vice-President.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

**Reason (R):** Ministers are elected by the Rajya Sabha and can be removed only by it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: the Council answers to the Lok Sabha, which can remove it by a no-confidence motion. R is false: the Prime Minister is appointed by the President and the ministers are chosen on the Prime Minister's advice; the Rajya Sabha neither elects nor removes them.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Civil servants must resign whenever a new party forms the government.

**Reason (R):** Civil servants are recruited on merit and are expected to serve every government with political neutrality.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: civil servants are the permanent executive and stay in service when governments change. R is true, and it is precisely why they do not resign.

questions.stem_md: The President of India is elected directly by all adult citizens in a nationwide vote.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The President is elected indirectly, by an electoral college of elected members of Parliament and the State Legislative Assemblies.

questions.stem_md: An officer of the Indian Police Service who was recruited by the Union can be posted to serve in a state.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The Indian Police Service is an All India Service: recruited by the Union but serving in the states.

questions.stem_md: In the presidential system of Arvelia, the legislature can remove the President simply by passing a vote of no confidence on a policy dispute.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** In a presidential system the President holds a fixed term and does not depend on the confidence of the legislature; removal, where possible, needs a special process such as impeachment. A no-confidence vote is a feature of parliamentary systems.

questions.stem_md: The ___ Amendment, passed in 2003, limited the size of the Council of Ministers to 15 per cent of the strength of the Lok Sabha.
questions.solution_md: The 91st Amendment (2003) capped the Council of Ministers at 15 per cent of the strength of the House; a similar limit applies in the states.

questions.stem_md: The President of India is elected by proportional representation by means of the system of single transferable ___.
questions.solution_md: The system is proportional representation by single transferable vote, with a secret ballot.

questions.stem_md: The President of India holds office for a term of ___ years.
questions.solution_md: The term is five years, and the Vice-President also has a five-year term.

questions.stem_md: Match each type of executive with an example.

options.text_md: Presidential
Parliamentary
Semi-presidential

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(r), (c)–(p). The United States has a presidential executive, the United Kingdom (like India) a parliamentary one and France a semi-presidential one.

questions.stem_md: Match each part of the executive or the services with its description.

options.text_md: All India Services
Central Services
State Services
Political executive

match_right.text_md: Ministers who are elected and hold office for a time
Recruited by the Union and serving in the states
Recruited by a State Public Service Commission

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each description fits one category; the political executive is the elected, temporary part, unlike the three kinds of civil service.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps in the order in which they would happen after an imagined general election with no clear majority.

options.text_md: The government faces the Lok Sabha to prove its majority
The President invites the leader who seems able to command majority support
The leader is appointed Prime Minister and the ministers take oath
The result gives no party or alliance a clear majority in the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The hung result comes first, then the President's choice, then the appointment, and finally the test of support in the House.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these four developments concerning the Union executive in the order in which they happened.

options.text_md: The Council of Ministers is limited to 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha
The President is allowed to return the advice once for reconsideration
The ministers' advice is made binding on the President
The Constitution comes into force with a parliamentary executive

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). The Constitution came into force in 1950, the 42nd Amendment in 1976, the 44th Amendment in 1978 and the 91st Amendment in 2003.

questions.stem_md: What is the executive? Distinguish the political executive from the permanent executive.
questions.solution_md: A definition of the executive and the two-part distinction.

answer.model_answer_md: The **executive** is the branch of government that puts laws and policies into effect. Its **political** part is made up of elected ministers and the head of government, who hold office for a time. Its **permanent** part is made up of **civil servants**, who remain in service under every government.

marking_scheme.step: Political executive elected and temporary; permanent executive civil servants

questions.stem_md: Why is the President of India called a nominal head of the executive?
questions.solution_md: Power exercised in the name of the President but by the Council; advice is binding.

answer.model_answer_md: Executive power is exercised in the **President's name**, but in practice by the **Council of Ministers**, whose advice the President must follow. The real executive is therefore the Prime Minister and the Council, while the President is the **constitutional head**.

marking_scheme.step: Power is exercised in the President's name by the Council of Ministers
The President must act on the Council's advice

questions.stem_md: State the role of the Union Public Service Commission and one safeguard of its independence.
questions.solution_md: Recruitment role and security of tenure.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Union Public Service Commission** recruits officers for the Union services, including the All India Services, through examinations on merit. Its members have **security of tenure**, so they cannot be removed at will by the government, which helps them to act independently.

marking_scheme.step: Recruits for the Union services on merit

questions.stem_md: Name the members of the electoral college that elects the President of India and the method of voting.
questions.solution_md: The members of the college and the method of voting.

answer.model_answer_md: The college consists of the **elected members of both Houses of Parliament** and the **elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies**, including those of Delhi and Puducherry. Voting is by **proportional representation by single transferable vote**, through a secret ballot.

marking_scheme.step: Elected members of both Houses and of the State Legislative Assemblies
Proportional representation by single transferable vote

questions.stem_md: In an imagined session, the Lok Sabha passes a motion of no confidence against the government. Using the idea of collective responsibility, explain what follows and why.
questions.solution_md: The meaning of the term applied to a no-confidence motion.

answer.model_answer_md: The Council of Ministers is **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha**: it acts as one team and is jointly answerable for its decisions. When the House passes a **no-confidence motion**, the **whole Council must resign**, and not only the Prime Minister or one minister.

marking_scheme.step: Whole Council jointly responsible; stands or falls together
Owed to the Lok Sabha; no confidence means resignation

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the Vice-President of India.
questions.solution_md: Chair of the Rajya Sabha; acting as President.

answer.model_answer_md: The Vice-President is the **ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** and presides over its sittings. In addition, when the office of President falls vacant, the Vice-President **acts as President** until it is filled. The term of office is five years.

marking_scheme.step: Ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Acts as President when the office is vacant

questions.stem_md: Sheela Nair, an officer in the imagined state of Orvan, served one government and now serves a new government with quite different policies. Why is she expected to carry them out, and which feature of the civil service explains this?
questions.solution_md: Permanence and political neutrality applied to the officer.

answer.model_answer_md: Civil servants are the **permanent executive**: they stay when ministers change. They are recruited on merit and are **politically neutral**, so Sheela must **implement the policies of the government of the day** impartially, while advising the ministers frankly.

marking_scheme.step: Governments change but civil servants continue
They must implement any government's policies impartially

questions.stem_md: How does the Cabinet differ from the Council of Ministers?
questions.solution_md: The Council is the whole body; the Cabinet is the inner group.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Council of Ministers** is the whole body of ministers, of three ranks: Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers. The **Cabinet** is the smaller **inner group** of senior ministers, who take the major policy decisions of the government.

marking_scheme.step: Council of Ministers is the whole body of ministers
Cabinet is the smaller inner group taking major decisions

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Meghpur has a Legislative Assembly of 120 members. State the limit on its Council of Ministers, the Amendment that sets it, and how you reach the figure.
questions.solution_md: The Amendment, the rule and the calculation.

answer.model_answer_md: The **91st Amendment (2003)** limits the Council of Ministers to **15 per cent** of the strength of the House; a similar limit applies in the states. Fifteen per cent of 120 is **18**, so the Council of Meghpur, including the Chief Minister, can have at most 18 members.

marking_scheme.step: 91st Amendment (2003): 15 per cent of the House

questions.stem_md: How are Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes provided for in recruitment to government posts?
questions.solution_md: Reservation in recruitment with the Union figures.

answer.model_answer_md: The Constitution allows **reservation of posts** in public employment for these groups. In direct recruitment to Union posts the quotas are **15 per cent** for Scheduled Castes, **7.5 per cent** for Scheduled Tribes and **27 per cent** for Other Backward Classes (as of 2024); states fix their own.

marking_scheme.step: Reservation of posts in recruitment is provided
The Union figures: 15, 7.5 and 27 per cent

questions.stem_md: Describe the three categories of civil services in India.
questions.solution_md: Each category named with its recruiter and field of service.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **All India Services**, for example the Indian Administrative Service and the Indian Police Service, are recruited by the Union and posted in the states.
2. The **Central Services** work for the Union government and are filled through the Union Public Service Commission.
3. The **State Services** work for a state government and are filled through its State Public Service Commission.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the Prime Minister is appointed and to whom the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are responsible.
questions.solution_md: Appointment, the majority link and responsibility to the Lok Sabha.

answer.model_answer_md: The **President appoints** the Prime Minister, who is normally the **head of the majority group** in the Lok Sabha. The President names the other ministers on the Prime Minister's advice. The Prime Minister and the Council are **jointly answerable to the Lok Sabha**, which can remove them through a **no-confidence motion**.

marking_scheme.step: Appointed by the President as leader of the majority
Ministers appointed on the Prime Minister's advice
Collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha

questions.stem_md: Describe any three situations in which the President of India can use discretion in practice.
questions.solution_md: Three of the three recognised areas of discretion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The President may **return the advice** of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration.
2. The President may **delay assent** to an ordinary bill, since no time limit is set; this is the **pocket veto**.
3. When no party or alliance has a clear majority, the President uses **personal judgment** in choosing the Prime Minister.

marking_scheme.step: Choosing a Prime Minister in a hung House

questions.stem_md: State three concerns that some people raise about the working of the bureaucracy.
questions.solution_md: Three concerns, each framed as a view.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Some argue that there is **political interference**, such as pressure over postings and decisions.
2. Some argue that officers are not sufficiently **accountable to citizens**, since they are not directly elected.
3. Some argue that **red tape** delays work and that officers need to be more **responsive** to the needs of people.

questions.stem_md: Describe any three kinds of powers of the President of India with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Three of the four groups of powers with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Executive powers:** appointing the Prime Minister, judges and Governors.
2. **Legislative powers:** giving assent to bills, issuing ordinances and addressing Parliament.
3. **Financial and emergency powers:** a money bill can be introduced only with the President's recommendation, and the President can proclaim an emergency on the advice of the Council.

marking_scheme.step: Financial or emergency power with example

questions.stem_md: Compare the presidential and parliamentary types of executive in three points, using the imagined countries Arvelia and Brendoria.
questions.solution_md: Three contrasts: heads, responsibility, election.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In presidential Arvelia the President is **both head of state and head of government**; in parliamentary Brendoria the head of state is **nominal** and the Chancellor leads the government.
2. Arvelia's President has a **fixed term**; Brendoria's Cabinet needs the **confidence of the legislature**.
3. The Arvelian President is **directly elected**.

marking_scheme.step: Fixed term versus confidence of the legislature

questions.stem_md: Explain the semi-presidential type of executive with the example of France.
questions.solution_md: Both offices, the example and the sharing of power.

answer.model_answer_md: A **semi-presidential** executive has **both** a directly elected President and a Prime Minister. In **France** the President is elected by the people and holds real powers, while the **Prime Minister**, with the Cabinet, runs the government and is responsible to the legislature. The two share the executive.

marking_scheme.step: A directly elected President and a Prime Minister
The Prime Minister is responsible to the legislature

questions.stem_md: Distinguish the presidential, parliamentary and semi-presidential types of executive, with an example of each.
questions.solution_md: Each type with its example and a point on the location of power.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In the **presidential** type, as in the **United States**, the President is directly elected, is head of state and of government, and serves a fixed term.
2. In the **parliamentary** type, as in the **United Kingdom** and **India**, the Prime Minister and Cabinet are **responsible to the legislature** and can be removed by it.
3. The head of state in a parliamentary system is **nominal**.
4. In the **semi-presidential** type, as in **France**, there is both a **directly elected President** and a **Prime Minister**.
5. The three types differ in where real power lies and to whom the government answers.

marking_scheme.step: Parliamentary type with responsibility to the legislature
Nominal head in the parliamentary type

questions.stem_md: Explain how the President of India is elected, the term and removal, and the main powers of the office.
questions.solution_md: Electoral college, method, term and removal, and the four kinds of powers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The President is elected **indirectly** by an **electoral college** of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies.
2. Voting is by **proportional representation by single transferable vote**, in a secret ballot.
3. The term is **five years**, and the President can be removed by **impeachment** for violating the Constitution.
4. Powers are **executive** (appointing the Prime Minister, judges and Governors) and **legislative** (assent to bills, ordinances).
5. There are also **financial** and **emergency** powers, exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

questions.stem_md: Is the President of India only a figurehead? Discuss with reference to the advice of ministers and the discretion the President can use.
questions.solution_md: Both views, the two amendments, two areas of discretion and a reasoned conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Some argue that the President is a **figurehead**, since the **42nd Amendment (1976)** made the ministers' advice binding.
2. Others point out that the **44th Amendment (1978)** lets the President **return the advice once** for reconsideration.
3. The President may **delay assent** to an ordinary bill (the **pocket veto**), as there is no time limit.
4. In a **hung House**, the President uses judgment in choosing the Prime Minister.
5. The office is therefore **nominal in routine**, with limited but real discretion in special situations.

marking_scheme.step: Choice of Prime Minister in a hung House

questions.stem_md: Explain the position of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers in the Union executive.
questions.solution_md: Appointment, membership rule, responsibility, size limit and the Cabinet.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **President appoints** the **Prime Minister**, who heads the **majority group** in the Lok Sabha.
2. Every minister must belong to Parliament or join it **within six months** of appointment.
3. The Council is **collectively responsible** to the Lok Sabha and must resign if a **no-confidence motion** is passed.
4. The **91st Amendment (2003)** limits its size to **15 per cent** of the Lok Sabha.
5. The **Cabinet** is the inner group of senior ministers who take the main decisions.

marking_scheme.step: Appointment and leadership of the majority
Membership of Parliament within six months
The Cabinet as the inner group

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure and the role of the civil services as the permanent executive in India.
questions.solution_md: Features, role, three categories, commissions and reservation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Civil servants are the **permanent executive**: recruited on **merit**, trained, and expected to be **politically neutral**.
2. They **implement policies** and **advise ministers**.
3. The services are the **All India Services** (the Indian Administrative Service and Indian Police Service), the **Central Services** and the **State Services**.
4. The **Union Public Service Commission** recruits for the Union services and **State Public Service Commissions** for the states; their members have **security of tenure**.
5. Reservation exists in recruitment for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.

marking_scheme.step: Role: implement policy and advise ministers

questions.stem_md: Some argue that the bureaucracy needs reform. Examine the concerns raised and the arguments on the other side.
questions.solution_md: Three concerns, a counter-view and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Some argue that there is **political interference** in the work and postings of officers.
2. Some argue that officers are insufficiently **accountable to citizens**, since they are not elected.
3. Others argue that **red tape** slows work, and that officers must become more **responsive**.
4. On the other side, it is argued that **neutral officers with security of tenure** guard against hasty or partisan decisions, and that rules protect fairness.
5. A balanced view looks for **responsiveness without losing neutrality**.

marking_scheme.step: The other side: neutrality and rules protect fairness

questions.stem_md: Read the newspaper report and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined report written by SOYL for practice; the newspaper, the alliances and the places are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** A result with no majority group is called hung.

**(b)** The choice of Prime Minister in a hung House.

**(c) (i)** Link to responsibility to the Lok Sabha and the role of the House.

**OR (c) (ii)** The need for majority support and the possibility of no confidence.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A **hung House** (a hung Lok Sabha).

**(b)** The President used **personal judgment in choosing the Prime Minister**, since no group had a clear majority.

**(c) (i)** The Prime Minister and Council are **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha**, so they can govern only with its **confidence**. The President's judgment is provisional, and the House settles whether the government has **majority support**.

**OR (c) (ii)** A Prime Minister who lacks **majority support** in the Lok Sabha would be removed by a **no-confidence motion**. The President must therefore choose the person **most likely to command the House**, within the limits of the **parliamentary system**.

questions.passage_md:

The President then invited the leader whose letters showed the widest support and asked the new government to prove its majority in the Lok Sabha within ten days.

The House decides on majority support

alternatives.solution_md: The need for majority support and the possibility of no confidence.

answer.model_answer_md: A Prime Minister who lacks **majority support** in the Lok Sabha would be removed by a **no-confidence motion**. The President must therefore choose the person **most likely to command the House**, within the limits of the **parliamentary system**.

The President must choose who can command the House

questions.stem_md: Read the diary extract and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined diary written by SOYL for practice; the officer, the district and the people are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The Union commission recruits for the All India Services.

**(b)** A file that moves slowly through many desks.

**(c) (i)** Neutrality and resistance to interference.

**OR (c) (ii)** One reason and one counter-argument.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **Union Public Service Commission**.

**(b)** **Red tape**: delay caused by many procedures and desks.

**(c) (i)** Civil servants must act on **rules and merit**, not to please politicians. By refusing to move the clerk to suit a request, she **resisted political interference** and treated staff impartially, as the permanent executive should.

questions.passage_md:
**From the imagined diary of Ritu Bhandari, an officer of the Indian Administrative Service posted as District Collector of Sundarpet**

9 a.m.: Reviewed the flood-relief plan that the state minister announced; my task is to carry it out in the 46 villages of the district.
12 noon: A local representative asked me to transfer a clerk who had not favoured his supporters. I explained that postings follow the rules and not requests.
3 p.m.: A pensioner came about a file that had passed through seven desks in two months. I felt ashamed of the delay.
6 p.m.: Sent the Secretary a note on the changes the department could make to speed up work.

**(b)** The Cabinet is the inner group of senior ministers.

**(c) (i)** The difference, and the Amendment.

questions.stem_md: Read the classroom discussion and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined discussion written by SOYL for practice; the school and the students are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The 44th Amendment (1978).

**(b)** The advice is then binding.

**(c) (i)** A reasoned judgment.

**OR (c) (ii)** Delayed assent and choice of the Prime Minister.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **44th Amendment**, in **1978**.

**(b)** The President must **act in accordance with the advice**.

**(c) (i)** It gives the President a **limited check**, as the Council must **think again**, but the final decision rests with the **Council of Ministers**. The office therefore remains **nominal** in the main, with some **discretion**.

**OR (c) (ii)** The President may **delay assent** to an ordinary bill, the **pocket veto**, because no time limit is set. And when no party or alliance has a clear majority, the President uses **judgment in choosing the Prime Minister**.
